t: Minimum Total Operations: Count Adjacent Differences
o: Each operation adds a constant k to a prefix. Consider the difference array d[i] = nums[i] − nums[i−1] for i ≥ 1: adding k to a prefix of length p changes exactly one difference, d[p], by −k (and shifts nothing else). Making all elements equal is equivalent to zeroing every d[i], i ≥ 1, and each operation fixes exactly one such d[i] (pick p = i, k = d[i]). Hence the answer is simply the count of nonzero adjacent differences. Check: [1,4,2] has d = [3,−2], both nonzero → 2 ✓; [10,10,10] → 0 ✓. nums[0]'s final value is absorbed for free into whichever operation touches prefix length ≥ 1.
k: Adding k to a prefix of length p toggles exactly one entry of the difference array: d[p] ← d[p] − k.
All-equal ⟺ all differences d[1..n−1] are zero; each operation can zero exactly one of them.
Therefore the minimum number of operations is the number of indices i with nums[i] ≠ nums[i−1].

a.i: Scan once and count positions where consecutive elements differ. Lower bound: each operation changes at most one difference, so #nonzero differences operations are necessary; the construction above shows they suffice.
s: For i from 1 to n−1, increment count when nums[i] != nums[i−1].
a.t: O(n) — single pass over the array

w: The difference-array viewpoint is the entire problem; a naive simulation (repeatedly normalizing prefixes) is O(n²) and unnecessary. Pitfalls: assuming the target value must be nums[0] or 0 (it can be anything — the first element rides along free), and off-by-one on whether the prefix of length n counts (it changes no difference, hence never helps). Edge cases: n = 1 (answer 0), all-equal arrays, extreme values (no arithmetic overflow risk since we only compare). Follow-up: minimum operations if you may only add positive k, or if operations affect suffixes instead.
